system_description.narrative_title: AI, Great-Power Engagement, Regional Wars and Market Strain
system_description.narrative_summary: The international system is being reshaped by an accelerating US–China engagement focused on AI, trade and strategic materials even as regional wars (Ukraine; Iran/Houthis vs. Gulf states) raise energy and security risks. Simultaneously, the rapid commercialization and militarization of AI, repeated high-profile cyber incidents, and fragile financial conditions (rising yields, debt issuance, stressed data‑centre financing) create cross-cutting vulnerabilities that tie technology, economics and geopolitics together. Domestic political turbulence in major democracies and shifting alliance moves in the Arctic and NATO add further unpredictability to decision cycles and crisis management.
system_description.scope: Interactions among major powers (US, China, Russia and their partners), regional conflict processes (Ukraine war; Iran-Houthi–Gulf confrontations), the global AI and cyber ecosystem (development, safety, militarization, hacks), international financial markets and corporate capital flows, and multilateral/diplomatic forums shaping crisis management and trade.
system_description.super_system: The global political-economic order: the integrated system of sovereign states, transnational markets, and multilateral institutions that governs security, trade, finance and technology.
adjacent_subsystems: Global energy and commodity markets (oil, gas, shipping, rare earths)
International financial system and capital markets (sovereign debt, bond markets, IPOs, corporate financing)
Global technology and cybersecurity ecosystem (AI labs, cloud/data-centre infrastructure, cybercrime)

variables.name: Russia-Ukraine high-intensity war
variables.description: Russia, Ukraine and NATO are locked in an escalating, multi-domain war — including long-range strikes, drones and economic warfare — that is shifting front lines, raising military commitments and straining European security.

variables.name: US–China strategic competition
variables.description: The United States and China are contesting trade, technology (chips, rare earths), diplomatic influence and security questions (including Taiwan and summit diplomacy), reshaping supply chains, alliances and global governance norms.

variables.name: Middle East escalation: Iran, Houthis and Gulf security
variables.description: Iran, Houthi forces, Saudi Arabia and external backers (notably the United States and regional partners) are engaged in an expanding cycle of missile/drone strikes, maritime disruption and proxy operations that threaten energy routes and regional stability.

variables.name: Global AI industrial race and governance
variables.description: Major tech firms and governments across the United States, Europe and Asia are racing to build far more powerful AI while negotiating safety standards, liability rules, export controls and industrial policy that will recast economic competition and national security frameworks.

variables.name: Global energy supply and fuels shock
variables.description: Producers, traders and consumers worldwide — including OPEC states, major exporters and energy-dependent economies — are grappling with a prolonged diesel/jet-fuel and tanker shortage driven by conflict, logistics bottlenecks and shifting sanctions, reallocating geopolitical leverage around energy chokepoints.
